title: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet
directAnswer: Merging two triplets replaces them with their component-wise max, so values only ever grow. The brute force tries subsets and merges them in exponential time. The greedy observation: any triplet with a component greater than the corresponding target value is poison — using it overshoots that axis forever. So keep only the 'safe' triplets (every component ≤ target), and check that for each of the three axes some safe triplet already equals the target there. If all three axes are hit, return true. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Greedy filter-then-cover — discard overshooters, hit each axis
remember.formula:
hit = [False, False, False]
for a, b, c in triplets:
    if a <= tx and b <= ty and c <= tz:   # safe triplet
        if a == tx: hit[0] = True
        if b == ty: hit[1] = True
        if c == tz: hit[2] = True
return all(hit)
rules: Merging is **component-wise max**, so a value can only **increase** — you can never bring an overshot axis back down.
A triplet with **any** component `> target` is unusable: include it and that axis overshoots permanently. **Filter it out.**
Among the **safe** triplets (all three components `≤ target`), you need each axis `k` to be **exactly equalled** by some safe triplet.
It's always safe to **merge every** safe triplet — none can push an axis past target, so greediness costs nothing.
Track three booleans (or a set) for 'axis x/y/z reached'; return true **iff all three** are hit.
No need to actually merge or build subsets — the question reduces to **three independent coverage checks**.
whenToUse: Combine operation is monotone (max/OR/union) so values only grow
A target must be matched component-wise across independent axes
Elements that exceed the target on any axis are strictly harmful and can be dropped
You can decompose 'can we build X' into per-coordinate coverage checks
antiSignals: The combine operation can decrease a value (min, subtraction) → filtering logic flips or breaks
Axes are coupled (a choice helping one axis forces another past target) → can't treat coordinates independently
You must return the actual subset used → track contributors, not just booleans
Targets aren't a fixed point of the operation → reframe the problem
remember.takeaway: Merge Triplets is the cleanest 'monotone combine + filter the poison' greedy: because max only grows, any triplet exceeding the target is forbidden, and once you keep only safe ones you can merge them all freely — the problem collapses to three independent 'did any safe triplet equal the target here?' checks. The same 'drop anything that can only overshoot' idea recurs wherever the combine operation is monotone.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reason about the monotonicity of the merge (max only increases) to conclude that overshooting triplets are unusable, and whether you then decompose a seemingly-coupled 3D problem into three independent per-axis coverage checks.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to enumerate which subset of triplets to merge (exponential), or forgetting to filter out triplets that exceed the target on some axis and then merging them — which silently overshoots and corrupts the result.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the monotonicity argument explicitly — 'merge is component-wise max, so a too-big component can never come back down, hence any triplet exceeding target is poison' — then prove both directions: every usable triplet is safe, and merging all safe triplets reproduces target exactly when each axis is covered.

problemStatement:
A triplet is an array of three integers. You are given a 2D integer array `triplets`, where `triplets[i] = [aᵢ, bᵢ, cᵢ]` describes the `i`-th triplet. You are also given an integer array `target = [x, y, z]` that describes the triplet you want to obtain.

To obtain `target`, you may apply the following operation any number of times:

- Choose two indices (0-indexed) `i` and `j` (`i != j`) and **update** `triplets[j]` to become `[max(aᵢ, aⱼ), max(bᵢ, bⱼ), max(cᵢ, cⱼ)]`.

Return `true` *if it is possible to obtain the* `target` *triplet* `[x, y, z]` *as an element of* `triplets`, *or* `false` *otherwise.*
constraints: 1 ≤ aᵢ, bᵢ, cᵢ, x, y, z ≤ 1000
Merging replaces a triplet with the component-wise max of two triplets
understanding: You can repeatedly fuse triplets by taking the per-component maximum, which only ever raises values. The question is whether some sequence of fusions can produce exactly target = [x, y, z]. Because order of merges doesn't matter and max is associative, this reduces to: is there a set of triplets whose component-wise max equals target?

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the order of merges matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — component-wise max is associative and commutative, so any sequence of merges over a chosen set yields the same result: the per-component max of that set. That's why we can think in terms of sets, not sequences.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can merging ever decrease a component?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Never. Each merge takes a max, so every component is monotone non-decreasing. That monotonicity is the entire basis for filtering out triplets that exceed the target.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I have to use a triplet exactly equal to target, or build it up?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: You can build it up from several triplets, each contributing the target value on at least one axis — as long as none of them exceeds the target anywhere.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are all values positive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, everything is in [1, 1000]. No negatives to complicate the max reasoning.

examples.explanation: [2,5,3] gives x=2, [1,7,5] gives y=7 and z=5. All three safe (≤ target). Merging them: [max(2,1), max(5,7), max(3,5)] = [2,7,5] = target.
Every triplet has a component exceeding target (b=4>2, etc.), so no safe triplet exists and the y-axis (2) can never be matched.
Safe triplets (all ≤ [5,5,5]): [2,5,3] hits y=5, [1,2,5] hits z=5, [5,2,3] hits x=5. Merging the three reproduces [5,5,5]. ([2,3,4] is also safe but unneeded.)

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Monotone merge means overshooters are poison; the rest reduces to three independent coverage checks.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Enumerate Subsets and Merge
approaches.whenToMention: Mention briefly to frame the search space, then immediately note 2ⁿ subsets is hopeless for n = 10⁵ and pivot to the structural insight.
hints: Since merge order doesn't matter, the result of merging a chosen set is just the component-wise max over that set. So the question is: does some subset have component-wise max equal to target?
The literal approach enumerates every subset, computes its component-wise max, and checks against target.
That's 2ⁿ subsets — astronomically too slow for n up to 10⁵. The point of writing it is to expose the structure that makes it collapsible.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are 2ⁿ subsets; computing the component-wise max of a subset costs up to O(n). The product O(2ⁿ · n) is exponential and infeasible beyond tiny n.
approaches.explanation:
Because merging is associative and commutative max, merging any chosen *set* of triplets yields exactly the component-wise maximum of that set. So 'can we obtain target?' is equivalent to 'does some subset of triplets have a component-wise max equal to `[x, y, z]`?'. The brute force answers that literally: enumerate every subset, fold it with max, and compare to target.

**Why subsets and not sequences.** A first instinct is to model the *sequence* of merge operations, but order is irrelevant — `max(max(a, b), c) = max(a, max(b, c))`. Collapsing sequences to sets removes a huge amount of redundant exploration, but it still leaves `2ⁿ` subsets to try.

**Why this is hopeless at scale.** With `n` up to `10⁵`, `2ⁿ` is beyond cosmic. Even at `n = 30` it's a billion subsets. We're not going to run this; we write it to *see the structure*: each subset is judged purely by, for each axis independently, the maximum value it contributes on that axis.

**Why the structure begs for a greedy.** Notice the three axes are evaluated *independently* under max — the x-coordinate of the merged result depends only on the x-coordinates of the chosen triplets, never on their y or z. That independence is the crack we pry open: instead of choosing a subset jointly, we can reason axis-by-axis about which triplets are even allowed to participate. The next approach turns that into an O(n) test.

**Why we keep the equivalence.** The subset framing is what justifies the greedy's correctness later: when we prove 'target is achievable iff each axis is covered by a safe triplet', we're really characterising exactly which subsets have component-wise max equal to target.
approaches.insight: Two reductions shrink the problem: merges → sets (order doesn't matter under max), and then sets → per-axis coverage (max evaluates each coordinate independently). The exponential brute force exists only to surface those two facts; once you see them, no enumeration is needed.

Triplet i is in this subset; fold it into the running component-wise max.

java.explanation: This subset's merge equals target — achievable.

python.explanation: Every non-empty subset, encoded as a bitmask.
Include triplet i and take component-wise max.
Subset reproduces target exactly → return True.

pitfalls: Modelling merge sequences instead of subsets — explodes the search even further for no reason.
Believing 2ⁿ could pass — it can't beyond ~n=20; this is illustrative only.
Including a triplet that overshoots target and still expecting a match — the merged max will exceed target.

approaches.name: Greedy — Filter Overshooters, Cover Each Axis (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'merge is monotone max, so any triplet bigger than target on any axis is poison — keep the rest and check each axis is hit'.
hints: Merging takes a max, so values only ever go up. If a triplet has a component larger than target's, including it overshoots that axis — and you can never bring it back down. What does that say about which triplets are usable?
Keep only 'safe' triplets: those with all three components ≤ target. Merging any collection of safe triplets can never exceed target on any axis.
Among safe triplets, you need each axis to actually reach the target value. Track three booleans: does some safe triplet equal target on x? on y? on z? Return true iff all three are covered.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass over n triplets with O(1) work each (three comparisons to test safety, three to update coverage) gives O(n) time; we keep three booleans, so O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Scan the triplets once. Call a triplet **safe** if `a ≤ x` and `b ≤ y` and `c ≤ z` — every component is within target. For each safe triplet, mark the axes on which it *equals* the target (`a == x` marks axis 0, and so on). After the pass, return `true` iff all three axes were marked.

**Why overshooting triplets are poison — the monotonicity argument.** Merging is component-wise max, so once any component exceeds its target value, no further merge can reduce it — max never decreases. Therefore if you ever fold a triplet with, say, `a > x` into your working set, the x-component is stuck above `x` forever and you can never equal target. So any triplet exceeding target on *any* axis is permanently unusable and must be discarded. Only safe triplets can participate.

**Why it's free to merge all safe triplets — and why that proves sufficiency.** Suppose for each axis there's a safe triplet equalling target there. Merge *all* safe triplets together. On axis x, the result is the max of `a` over all safe triplets; since every safe triplet has `a ≤ x`, that max is `≤ x`, and since some safe triplet has `a == x`, the max is exactly `x`. The identical argument gives `y` on axis 2 and `z` on axis 3. So the merged triplet is exactly `[x, y, z]` — target is achievable. Crucially, throwing *extra* safe triplets into the merge can never hurt: they're all bounded by target, so they can't push any axis past it. That's why greed (take every safe triplet) is risk-free.

**Why the condition is also necessary — the contradiction argument.** Suppose target is achievable but some axis, say x, is *not* covered by any safe triplet. The achieving subset's component-wise max must equal `x` on that axis, so some triplet in the subset has `a == x`. For the subset to produce target, every triplet in it must be safe (an overshooter would have pushed some axis past target, as argued). So that triplet is a safe triplet with `a == x` — contradicting 'no safe triplet covers x'. Hence every axis covered by the achieving solution is covered by a safe triplet, and our three booleans capture exactly that. Both directions together make the three-way coverage check an *exact* characterisation, not a heuristic.

**Why the axes can be treated independently.** Component-wise max evaluates each coordinate in isolation — the x-result depends only on x-values. So 'cover x', 'cover y', 'cover z' are three independent sub-questions, and a single triplet may help with several at once. That independence is what lets one linear pass with three flags replace the exponential subset search.

**Why this beats the brute force.** The brute force searches `2ⁿ` subsets; the greedy uses monotonicity to forbid overshooters and coordinate-independence to split into three trivial coverage checks, collapsing `O(2ⁿ·n)` to `O(n)` and `O(n)` space to `O(1)`.
approaches.insight: The whole problem hinges on one property: the combine operation (max) is *monotone*, so anything that overshoots the target can only ever stay overshot — it's strictly harmful and gets filtered. Once the poison is gone, the remaining triplets can all be merged with impunity, and a multi-dimensional target decomposes into independent per-coordinate coverage. Spotting 'monotone combine ⇒ drop overshooters' is the transferable trick.

diagrams.title: Why overshooters are poison
diagrams.caption: Merge is component-wise max, so a component above target can never come back down — such triplets are filtered before any coverage check.

edgeCases.behavior: Single safe triplet equals target on all three axes → hit = [T,T,T] → true.
Both overshoot (b=4>2, b=5>2) so no safe triplet exists; y-axis (2) never covered → false.
[1,3,4] safe but matches no axis; [2,5,8] safe and equals target on all axes → true.

pitfalls: Forgetting the safety filter and merging overshooting triplets — silently exceeds target on some axis.
Requiring a single triplet to equal target on all axes instead of covering axes across several safe triplets.
Returning true as soon as one axis is hit — all three must be covered.

commonMistakes: Trying to enumerate which subset of triplets to merge instead of using monotonicity to filter and cover.
Merging triplets that exceed the target on some axis — the max overshoots and can never come back down.
Expecting one triplet to match target on all three axes rather than combining several safe triplets.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping the overshoot filter
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you fold in a triplet with a component above target, the component-wise max permanently exceeds target on that axis — yet a naive coverage check might still report success.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Demanding a single all-axis match
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Target can be assembled from several safe triplets, each contributing one or more axes. Requiring one triplet to equal target everywhere rejects valid inputs.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning on the first axis covered
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Coverage of one axis says nothing about the other two. The answer is the conjunction of all three coverage flags, checked after the full pass.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# accumulate all three flags across the whole pass
return all(hit)

patternNote: Canonical 'monotone combine + filter the poison' greedy: because merging is component-wise max (values only grow), any triplet exceeding the target on any axis is permanently unusable and is discarded, after which a multi-axis target decomposes into independent per-coordinate coverage checks. Recognise it whenever the combine operation is monotone and a target must be matched coordinate-by-coordinate.
